name: Congo Rainforest
place: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Congo, Gabon and Cameroon
blurb: Elephants, apes and fruit trees: a forest that plants itself through its animals.
notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records. The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles on the Congo Basin and the African forest elephant.

nodes.desc: Strong equatorial sun drives growth, but little of it reaches the forest floor.
The Cuvette Centrale gets about 2,000 mm of rain a year, which keeps the forest and swamps wet.
Break down leaf litter and dead animals and return nutrients to the soil, but slowly in waterlogged peat.

link_ideas.what: Straw-coloured fruit bats migrate long distances across Africa

story: The Congo Basin holds the largest rainforest in Africa, 300 million hectares, second only to the Amazon, and acts as a global carbon sink. Forest elephants eat the leaves, seeds and fruit of at least 96 plants and spread seeds at least 5 km, helping keep the forest diverse.
matters: Forest elephants in Central Africa have fallen about 86% in 31 years and are now Critically Endangered. Eight sites in the basin are World Heritage sites, five of them listed as in danger.
